definition.text: An increase in the amount and quality of the goods and services a society produces.

facts.text: It is usually measured as the rise in an economy's output after adjusting for inflation, over a year or a longer period.
The growth rate is typically calculated from real GDP, real GDP per person, GNI per person or median income.
Growth is calculated in real, inflation-adjusted terms so that rising prices do not distort the picture.
Rising labor productivity, the value of output per unit of labor, has historically been the most important source of real growth per person.
Over long periods even small rates of growth, such as 2% a year, have large effects.
So far, economic growth and carbon dioxide emissions have been closely correlated across nations, though carbon emitted per unit of GDP varies widely.
Worries about growth's environmental harm have led some to argue for slower growth or for abandoning growth altogether.
Adam Smith pioneered modern growth theory in The Wealth of Nations in 1776, naming division of labour and capital accumulation as its main drivers.

definition.text: The factors that raise output per person: labor productivity, hours worked, the share of working-age people in work, and the share of people of working age.

facts.text: Output per person can be broken into output per hour of labor, hours worked, the participation rate and the share of working-age people in the population.
Robert Solow estimated that technological progress accounted for 80 percent of the long-term rise in US income per person, and more capital investment for only 20 percent.
More capital per worker raises output up to a point, but capital faces diminishing returns, partly because of the growing burden of depreciation.
Many analyses give a major role to human capital, the skills of the workforce, though it is hard to measure because it is built at home, at school and on the job.
Human capital helps growth only if the population is healthy and well nourished.
Laws that protected contracts and private property helped economies move toward capitalism.
Moving workers from low-productivity farming to high-productivity manufacturing raised overall output.

title: Growth and the environment

definition.text: The argument over whether continued economic growth can be squared with the health of the planet's natural resources and ecosystems.

facts.text: Critics such as the Club of Rome argue that a narrow focus on growth, with globalization, risks a systemic collapse of natural resources.
Academics have proposed ideas such as uneconomic growth, a steady-state economy, eco-taxes, green investment and degrowth in response.
IPBES's 2019 Global Assessment warned that, given heavy biodiversity loss, society should not focus solely on economic growth.
Optimists argue that large-scale ecological effects of growth are minor; Julian Simon said in 1981 that human ingenuity would adapt to any that exist.
Partha Dasgupta's 2021 review for the British Treasury argued that human demands far exceed nature's capacity and called for abandoning GDP as the measure of success.
A 2019 warning signed by 11,000 scientists named economic growth as the driving force behind overexploitation of ecosystems.
Growth-oriented environmental economists instead propose government action to shift energy production toward wind, solar, hydroelectric and nuclear power.

contested_note: Sources disagree on whether growth's large-scale ecological effects are minor and adaptable or are driving ecosystem collapse.

definition.text: The idea that economic growth improves quality of life only up to a threshold point, after which further growth can make it worse.

facts.text: The idea produces an upside-down U-shaped curve whose peak marks the level of growth to aim for.
Happiness has been shown to rise with GDP per person at least up to $15,000 per person.
Health, education and political freedoms sometimes fail to improve as an economy grows.

title: Inequality and growth

definition.text: The question of whether unequal income and wealth help or hinder a country's economic growth.

facts.text: The classical view, from Adam Smith, held that inequality boosts saving by the wealthy and so speeds capital accumulation and growth.
Galor and Zeira argued that with imperfect credit markets inequality harms investment in skills and slows growth, except in very poor economies.
Galor and Moav suggest inequality helped early industrial growth but became harmful once human capital replaced physical capital as the main engine.
Thomas Piketty argued in 2013 that when the return on capital exceeds the growth rate of output, inequality rises.

contested_note: Classical, neoclassical and modern theories give opposite answers on whether inequality helps or hurts growth.

definition.text: The total market value of all final goods and services a country produces in a set period, usually a year.

facts.text: GDP is often used to measure a country's or region's economic activity and to compare countries.
Its major components are consumption, government spending, investment and net exports.
GDP is not a measure of overall living standards or well-being, since it ignores how income is shared.
It has been criticized for leaving out resource extraction, environmental impact and unpaid domestic work.
Simon Kuznets developed the modern concept for a 1934 US Congress report, warning against using it to measure welfare.
After the Bretton Woods Conference in 1944, GDP became the main tool for measuring a country's economy.
William Petty came up with an early concept of GDP to calculate the tax burden during the Anglo-Dutch wars of 1652 to 1674.
The international standard for measuring GDP is the System of National Accounts (2008), prepared by the IMF, EU, OECD, UN and World Bank.

title: Ways of measuring GDP
article: Gross domestic product#Determining gross domestic product (GDP)

definition.text: The production, income and expenditure approaches, three ways of measuring GDP that should in theory give the same total.

facts.text: The production approach, the most direct, adds up the output of every class of enterprise.
Also called the value-added approach, it counts how much value is contributed at each stage of production.
The income approach sums the primary incomes paid out by producers; measured this way it is called gross domestic income.
The expenditure approach adds up final uses of goods and services, leaving out intermediate consumption.
Within each country GDP is normally measured by a national statistical agency.

title: GDP expenditure components
article: Gross domestic product#Components of GDP by expenditure

definition.text: The breakdown of GDP as consumption plus investment plus government spending plus exports minus imports: Y = C + I + G + (X − M).

facts.text: Consumption, households' private spending, is normally the largest component.
Investment means spending on things like new equipment, buildings and software, not buying shares or bonds, which counts as saving.
Government spending covers final goods and services such as public salaries, but not transfer payments like unemployment benefits.
Imports are subtracted because they already appear in C, I and G and must not be counted as domestic supply.
Only spending on final goods counts; intermediate goods used to make other products are left out.

title: Nominal and real GDP
article: Gross domestic product#Nominal GDP and real GDP

definition.text: Nominal GDP is measured at the prices of the time, while real GDP is adjusted for changes in the value of money so years can be compared.

facts.text: Nominal GDP uses current market prices and so does not account for inflation.
If GDP rose from $100 million to $300 million while inflation halved money's value, real GDP grew 50 percent, not 200 percent.
The factor used to convert GDP from current to constant values is called the GDP deflator.
Real GDP is used to calculate the GDP growth rate, usually expressed as a percentage change from the previous year.

definition.text: GDP divided by the number of people in a country, measuring average production per person.

facts.text: Its main advantage as a living-standards indicator is that it is measured frequently, widely and consistently across countries.
Adjusted for purchasing power parity, it can help compare living standards between nations.
Like total GDP it ignores income distribution and tends to overstate the income of a typical person.
Median income growth has diverged from GDP per capita growth in some countries.

definition.text: The criticisms that GDP leaves out much of what shapes living standards, such as pollution, unpaid work, health and how income is shared.

facts.text: GDP ignores negative externalities: industrial output may raise GDP while the pollution it causes is not counted.
It excludes non-market activity such as household production, barter and volunteer work.
Estimates of unpaid work's value range from about 15% of GDP in Canada to nearly 70% in the United Kingdom.
Kuznets warned in 1937 that a nation's welfare can scarcely be inferred from national income.
GDP counts spending that would shrink if problems were solved, such as medical care and crime-fighting.
Robert F. Kennedy said GNP measures everything except that which makes life worthwhile.
The parable of the broken window notes that GDP treats spending on repairs as a net benefit, ignoring the original destruction.

definition.text: The criticism that GDP rewards activities that harm the environment and fails to show natural capital being used up.

facts.text: A traffic jam can raise GDP through extra fuel use while the resulting air pollution goes uncounted.
GDP may not show how much natural capital an economy is building or protecting.
The UK's Natural Capital Committee said in 2013 that GDP focuses on flows, not stocks, so an economy can run down its assets while recording high growth.
Deforestation, strip mining and overfishing are counted as activity in GDP despite long-term harm.
In 1989 John Cobb and Herman Daly introduced the Index of Sustainable Economic Welfare, which subtracts environmental degradation and natural capital depreciation.
China launched Gross Ecosystem Product in 2020 to measure ecosystems' contribution to the economy, including climate regulation.

definition.text: GDP measured by adding up the primary incomes paid out by producers in a country.

facts.text: Gross domestic income should give the same total as the expenditure method.

definition.text: The ability to consume and save that a person, household or firm gains over a set period, usually counted in money.

facts.text: Income is hard to define and its meaning differs between fields; economic income can differ from income as defined by law.
US tax law counts wages, salary, profit, interest, rent and other earnings received in a calendar year as household income.
For a firm, gross income can be defined as all revenue minus the cost of goods sold.
Borrowing or repaying money is not income under any definition, but interest and forgiven debt are.
Non-monetary joys, such as watching a sunset, are not counted as income, so reported income may misstate well-being.
Education raises income by increasing workers' skills and productivity.
Income is conventionally written as Y in economics.

definition.text: A widely used economic definition of income as consumption plus the change in a person's net worth.

facts.text: The definition dates from 1938 and counts both what is consumed and the change in the value of property held.
Taxable income is usually lower than Haig–Simons income, since unrealized gains such as a rise in share prices are economic but not taxable income.
'Full income' adds non-monetary consumption ability to money income, but it cannot be observed, forcing reliance on money income.

definition.text: The income earned from the factors of production: rent from land, wages from labor, interest from capital and profit from enterprise.

facts.text: In consumer theory, income is the budget a person can spend on different goods at their given prices.
National income is divided among the factors of production through the factor market.

definition.text: The extent to which income is spread unevenly across a population.

facts.text: It can be measured with tools such as the Lorenz curve and the Gini coefficient.
Many economists argue some inequality is necessary but excessive inequality causes efficiency problems and social injustice.
UN Sustainable Development Goal 10 aims to reduce inequality.
Globalization tends to raise a country's average income, but unequally.

title: Measures of national income and output
article: Measures of national income and output

definition.text: The family of statistics, such as GDP, GNI and net national income, used to estimate the total economic activity of a country or region.

facts.text: All of them count the total goods and services produced within an economy and its sectors.
Adjusted national income is net national income corrected for the depletion of natural resources.
Systematic national accounts began only in the 1930s in the United States and some European countries, spurred by the Great Depression and Keynesian economics.
Goods and services are counted at market value, the price they fetch, not their actual usefulness.
Three methods give market values for all output: the product, expenditure and income methods.
Some measures count only goods and services exchanged for money, while others impute values for bartered goods.

distinct_from: National income as a welfare measure

sources.title: Measures of national income and output

title: Avoiding double counting
article: Measures of national income and output#Output

definition.text: The rule that national output counts only the final value of a good, or the value added at each stage, not every sale along the chain.

facts.text: If meat is worth $10 at the farm, $30 at the butcher and $60 at the supermarket, $60 enters national output, not the $100 sum.
The values added at each stage, $10, $20 and $30, sum to the same final value.
GDP at market price equals the value of output minus intermediate consumption.

distinct_from: Measures of national income and output
National income as a welfare measure

sources.title: Measures of national income and output

title: Gross, net, domestic and national
article: Measures of national income and output#Expenditure

definition.text: The naming scheme of national income measures, combining gross or net, national or domestic, and product, income or expenditure.

facts.text: 'Gross' means total product, while 'net' subtracts the amount needed to offset depreciation of fixed capital.
'Domestic' counts everything produced inside a country's borders; 'national' counts everything produced by its nationals anywhere.
A French-owned cotton factory in Senegal counts in Senegal's domestic figures but France's national figures.
Net domestic product is GDP minus depreciation of capital.

distinct_from: Measures of national income and output
National income as a welfare measure

sources.title: Measures of national income and output

title: National income as a welfare measure
article: Measures of national income and output#National income and welfare

definition.text: The question of how well GDP per person reflects people's welfare, given what it leaves out.

facts.text: Countries with higher GDP may also score higher on other welfare measures such as life expectancy.
A paid nanny's income counts in GDP, but a parent's unpaid childcare does not.
Cleaning up an oil spill adds to GDP, while the lost well-being from fouled beaches is not measured.
Alternatives include the Human Development Index, Index of Sustainable Economic Welfare, Genuine Progress Indicator and sustainable national income.

distinct_from: Measures of national income and output

sources.title: Measures of national income and output

definition.text: An abundance of valuable assets or possessions that can be turned into a form usable in exchange.

facts.text: In economics, wealth is the net worth of a person, household or nation: the value of all assets owned minus all liabilities owed at a point in time.
The UN's inclusive wealth is a money measure adding up natural, human and physical assets.
Natural capital includes land, forests, energy resources and minerals; human capital is people's education and skills; physical capital is machinery, buildings and infrastructure.
Adam Smith described wealth as 'the annual produce of the land and labor of the society'.
Scarcity is a fundamental factor: a commodity freely available to everyone gives its owner no potential for wealth.
Wealth falls into three main categories: personal property, monetary savings, and income-producing capital such as real estate, stocks and businesses.
Global household wealth was estimated at US$418.3 trillion at the end of 2020, excluding human capital.
For 2018 the World Bank valued the world's produced, natural and human capital at $1,152 trillion.

definition.text: The distinction between wealth, a stock measured at a point in time, and income, a flow measured per unit of time.

facts.text: Wealth is like the value of an orchard on December 31 minus the debt owed on it.
Income is like the value of apples the orchard yields each year; measuring it per unit of time makes it a flow.
For national wealth in the national accounts, the liabilities that count are those owed to the rest of the world.
The wealth effect is the rise in total consumption that follows a rise in national wealth.

definition.text: How a society's or the world's total wealth is shared among people and regions.

facts.text: The Kuznets curve holds that inequality of wealth and income rises in early development, stabilizes, then falls.
In 2008 about 1% of adults were estimated to hold 40% of world wealth, or 32% adjusted for purchasing power parity.
In 2013, 1% of adults were estimated to hold 46% of world wealth.
Some adults have negative net worth, with debts larger than assets.

definition.text: A model of the economy showing the main exchanges as flows of money, goods and services between economic actors.

facts.text: Money and goods flow around a closed circuit in matching amounts but opposite directions.
In its simplest form, households supply labor to businesses and spend the income they earn on the goods and services businesses produce.
Circular flow analysis is the basis of national accounts and so of macroeconomics.
Richard Cantillon described the idea in 1730, and François Quesnay first visualized it in his 1758 Tableau économique.
Frank Knight drew the first modern circular flow diagram in 1933.
It shows that activities depend on one another: without consumption there is no demand, which limits production and income.

title: Circular flow sector models
article: Circular flow of income#Types of models

definition.text: The versions of the circular flow model with two to five sectors, built up by adding government, the rest of the world and finance to households and firms.

facts.text: The two-sector model has only households and firms, with households spending all their income on firms' output.
The three-sector model adds government; the four-sector model adds foreign trade and capital flows.
The five-sector model adds banks and other intermediaries that borrow household savings and lend for firms' investment.

title: Leakages and injections
article: Circular flow of income#Leakages and injection

definition.text: Leakages are money withdrawn from the circular flow, such as savings, taxes and imports; injections are money added, such as investment, government spending and exports.

facts.text: Saved money is a leakage because it is not spent, so not all output gets bought.
Taxes are a leakage; government spending on services and welfare payments is the matching injection.
Equilibrium in the five-sector model comes when total leakages equal total injections: savings + taxes + imports = investment + government spending + exports.

title: Circular flow and the environment
article: Circular flow of income#Circular flow diagram as a subsystem of the environment

definition.text: The critique that the circular flow model treats the economy as self-sustaining, when it really depends on a one-way throughput of matter and energy from the environment.

facts.text: The model implies the economy runs like a perpetual motion machine, which the laws of thermodynamics rule out.
No economy can recycle its own waste without new energy, so it must operate as a subsystem of a larger ecosystem.
Low-entropy matter and energy enter from natural capital such as solar energy, oil wells, fisheries and mines, and leave as high-entropy waste.
Because these inputs and the capacity to absorb waste are finite, there is a sustainable limit to the economy's growth.
Ecological economics replaces the simple circular flow with a diagram that includes solar energy and the natural inputs and services it sustains.

definition.text: A statistical estimate of the price level of the goods and services households buy, calculated as the weighted average price of a market basket.

facts.text: Prices are collected, often monthly, from a sample of shops and service businesses.
The annual percentage change in the CPI is used as a measure of inflation.
The CPI is used to adjust wages, salaries and pensions for inflation and to convert money amounts into real values.
The items in the basket are updated from time to time to follow changes in spending habits.
When an item is replaced by one of different quality, its price may be adjusted so the index shows price change rather than quality change.
It is not a perfect measure of inflation or the cost of living, but it is a useful tool for tracking them.
Hedonic regression is used in building the CPI.

definition.text: The way a consumer price index combines price changes for different goods, giving each a weight that reflects its share of consumer spending.

facts.text: In one example, housing carries 41.4% of the weight, food and beverages 17.4% and transport 17.0%.
Weights should ideally reflect current spending but in practice use the most recent past data.
Infrequent reweighting saves money but delays new kinds of spending, such as Internet subscriptions, from entering the index.

title: Owner-occupied housing in the CPI
article: Consumer price index#Owner-occupiers and the price index

definition.text: The long-running controversy over how a consumer price index should count the cost of living in a home one owns.

facts.text: Many economists argue the index should include the opportunity cost of living in one's own home.
A spending approach would count repairs, maintenance and also mortgage interest.
A transaction-price approach would count only purchases of new dwellings, like other durable goods.

contested_note: Statisticians and economists disagree on which of the competing methods should be used.

definition.text: The use of resources to meet present needs and wants, as opposed to investing for future income.

facts.text: Mainstream economists count only final purchases of newly produced goods and services by individuals for immediate use as consumption.
In most countries consumption is the largest part of GDP, usually between 45% and 85% of it.
In macroeconomics, consumption equals income minus savings.
Economists consider income the most important factor affecting consumption.
In microeconomics, consumers are assumed to choose goods to maximize their utility within their budget.
Aggregate consumption is a component of aggregate demand.

definition.text: Keynes's idea, also called the absolute income hypothesis, that consumer spending is a linear function of current disposable income.

facts.text: Keynes introduced the consumption function in his 1936 General Theory.
He held that real income is the most important influence on consumption in the short run.
Autonomous consumption is the minimum a household always consumes, by drawing down savings or borrowing.
Because it ignores future income, its critics developed the permanent income and life-cycle hypotheses.

definition.text: James Duesenberry's 1949 theory that people's consumption depends on their income relative to others, not only on its level.

facts.text: It assumes people's consumption choices are not independent of one another.
Two people with the same income but different positions in the income distribution will consume differently.

definition.text: Milton Friedman's theory that consumption depends on a person's long-run permanent income rather than temporary swings in income.

facts.text: Friedman set it out in the 1950s in A Theory of the Consumption Function.
Income is split into transitory and permanent parts, and changes in each affect consumption differently.
A change in permanent income changes consumption by the marginal propensity to consume times that change.

definition.text: Franco Modigliani's theory that people plan consumption using past, current and expected future income, spreading it over their lifetime.

facts.text: The source dates its publication by Modigliani to 1966.
It grew out of criticism that the Keynesian consumption function ignores future income.

definition.text: The idea, from the New Home Economics, that market consumption must be studied alongside the goods and services households produce for themselves.

facts.text: The opportunity cost of time changes the cost of home-made substitutes and so the demand for bought goods and services.
GDP excludes household production such as unpaid childcare.

definition.text: The link between what and how much people consume and their impact on the environment.

facts.text: What people eat and wear, the homes they live in and where they shop all affect the environment.
Consumption patterns changed drastically with the Industrial Revolution, as cheap mass-produced goods met rising wages.
Overconsumption, pollution and climate change can devastate biodiversity.
Researchers have found affluence to be the key driver of carbon emissions.

definition.text: The national-accounts term for the depreciation of fixed assets: the fall in their current value over a period through wear, normal obsolescence and normal accidental damage.

facts.text: It is valued at current market prices rather than historic cost, which is why the System of National Accounts avoids the word depreciation.
The UN manual says it may account for 10 per cent or more of total GDP.
Net measures such as net domestic product and net national income are found by deducting it from GDP and GNI.
Net national income shows the income actually available for consumption and new investment, making it a better measure of economic welfare than GDP.
It excludes the depletion or degradation of non-produced assets such as land, mineral deposits, coal, oil and natural gas.
It also excludes assets destroyed by war or rare major natural disasters.
Critics note that its 'economic' valuation yields figures that differ from standard accounting practice.

title: Capital consumption allowance
article: Consumption of fixed capital#Capital Consumption Allowance

definition.text: The part of GDP due to depreciation, measuring what a country must spend just to maintain, rather than grow, its productive capacity.

facts.text: It covers wear and tear on physical capital plus the investment needed to maintain human capital, such as educating workers to replace retirees.
GDP equals net domestic product plus the capital consumption allowance.

definition.text: In accounting, the fall in an asset's value as it is used and wears out, and the spreading of its original cost over the years it is useful.

facts.text: Businesses depreciate long-term assets for both accounting and tax purposes.
Depreciation reduces reported net income but does not require a current outlay of cash.
Depletion and amortization are the matching ideas for natural resources such as oil and for intangible assets.
An unexpected fall in an asset's value is recorded as an impairment charge.

definition.text: The ways of calculating depreciation, based either on the passage of time or on how much an asset is used.

facts.text: Straight-line depreciation, the simplest and most common, divides cost minus salvage value by the years of useful life.
Declining-balance and sum-of-years-digits methods write off more in early years, assuming assets are most productive when new.
Units-of-production depreciation charges more in years of heavy use; an asset costing $70,000 with $10,000 salvage value expected to make 6,000 units depreciates $10 per unit.

definition.text: The gradual loss in economic value of the capital stock of a firm or nation through physical wear, obsolescence or falling demand for what the capital provides.

facts.text: Next period's capital stock equals this period's stock plus gross investment minus depreciation.
Gross investment minus depreciation is net investment, the net addition to the capital stock.
Economic depreciation is the fall in the present value of the services an asset will provide in future.
An asset's value can rise instead, for example if the price of its services rises unexpectedly or the discount rate falls.
In national accounts it is called consumption of fixed capital, equal to the gap between gross and net fixed capital formation.
In the Solow–Swan growth model, a steady state occurs when gross investment equals depreciation.

definition.text: A government's use of taxes and spending to influence the economy.

facts.text: It grew out of the Great Depression of the 1930s, when the earlier hands-off approach to managing the economy stopped working.
It rests on Keynes's theory that changing taxes and government spending shifts aggregate demand and economic activity.
Fiscal policy handles taxes and spending, usually through a government department; monetary policy handles money supply and interest rates, usually through a central bank.
It is used to stabilize the economy over the business cycle.
Spending can be funded by taxes, by printing money (seigniorage) or by borrowing at home or abroad.
A fiscal deficit is often funded by issuing bonds; if revenue cannot cover the interest, a nation may default.
Developing countries collect about half as much tax as a share of GDP as developed countries, which limits their fiscal policy.

definition.text: The three settings of fiscal policy: neutral, expansionary and contractionary.

facts.text: Neutral policy keeps deficit spending about at its long-run average, typically when the economy is neither in recession nor boom.
Expansionary policy, used in recessions, means spending exceeds tax revenue by more than usual, through public works or tax cuts.
Contractionary policy raises taxes and cuts spending to cool growth that is causing excessive inflation.
Because tax revenue rises and falls with the business cycle, stances are judged on cyclically adjusted figures.

title: Monetary versus fiscal policy

definition.text: The debate over the relative strengths of central-bank monetary policy and government fiscal policy for steering the economy.

facts.text: Monetary policy is quicker to change, since interest rates can be set monthly, and is shielded from election politics.
In a liquidity trap, interest-rate cuts fail to boost demand because banks will not lend and consumers will not spend.
In a deep recession, monetary policy alone is not enough; government spending can kick-start demand.
Fiscal policy appears to have a greater long-run effect, while monetary policy tends to succeed in the short run.

contested_note: Economists weigh the two tools differently and still debate their effectiveness.

title: Effects of fiscal stimulus

definition.text: The question of how government spending increases and tax cuts change demand, prices, interest rates and output.

facts.text: Keynesians argue expansionary fiscal policy in recessions builds the base for growth and full employment, with deficits repaid by the later expansion.
In the IS-LM model, fiscal expansion raises the price level and real interest rates in the long run.
The AD-AS model lets the price level vary, making it better for long-run analysis.
Economists still debate how effective fiscal stimulus is.

contested_note: The sources say economists still debate the effectiveness of fiscal stimulus.

definition.text: A price index covering all new, domestically produced final goods and services, used to turn nominal GDP into real GDP.

facts.text: It equals nominal GDP divided by real GDP, times 100; the base year's value is 100.
Unlike the CPI, it has no fixed basket: the basket changes each year with spending and investment patterns.
A deflator of 200 means prices have doubled since the base year; one of 50 means they have halved.
In practice it usually differs only slightly from the CPI, but even small gaps can shift budgets.

definition.text: A measure of how unequally income, wealth or consumption is spread across a nation or group, from 0 for perfect equality to 1 for perfect inequality.

facts.text: Corrado Gini published it in 1912, building on Max Lorenz's work.
It is usually defined from the Lorenz curve, which plots the share of total income earned by the bottom share of the population; the 45-degree line is perfect equality.
With just two income groups, if the high earners are a share u of people and earn a share f of income, the Gini is f − u.
It can be calculated on market income, before taxes and transfers, or on disposable income.
In ecology it has been used to measure biodiversity, plotting the cumulative share of species against the cumulative share of individuals.
UNICEF put Latin America and the Caribbean's net income Gini at 48.3 in 2008, the highest of any region.

definition.text: The weaknesses of the Gini coefficient as a measure of inequality.

facts.text: It is a relative measure, so it can rise even while the number of people in absolute poverty falls.
It is not additive, and different income distributions can share the same value.
A population can have a very low income Gini and a very high wealth Gini at once.
Small populations with less varied economies tend to report lower values.

title: Global income inequality over time
article: Gini coefficient#World income Gini index since 1800s

definition.text: The long-run trend in income inequality among all the world's people.

facts.text: The global income Gini rose steadily from 1820 to 2002, with a sharp increase between 1980 and 2002.
The trend appears to have peaked and started to reverse with rapid growth in emerging economies such as the BRIC countries.

notes: Source sentence 5b5b90d12f3f says inequality 'will keep on increasing', while faa321727ed5 says the trend appears to have peaked and reversed; verify.

definition.text: The total factor income earned by a country's residents, formerly called gross national product (GNP).

facts.text: GNI equals GDP plus factor income residents receive from abroad, minus factor income paid to non-residents.
GDP defines its scope by location, GNI by ownership; for the whole world the two are the same.
Unlike GDP, GNI is a concept of income rather than of value added.
Net national income is GNI minus depreciation.
The 1993 revision of the System of National Accounts renamed GNP as GNI.
The United States used GNP as its main measure until 1991, when it switched to GDP.
It includes wages of cross-border and seasonal workers abroad but not remittances sent home, which is why France's GNI exceeds its GDP.
Ireland's GDP became so distorted by multinational profit shifting that in 2017 its central bank adopted a modified GNI measure.

definition.text: The knowledge, skills, know-how, health and education people bring to producing goods and services.

facts.text: It has a substantial effect on individual earnings, and investing in it yields high returns through childhood and young adulthood.
Adam Smith counted 'the acquired and useful abilities' of a society's members as capital; Irving Fisher may have first used the term.
Pigou wrote that there is investment in human capital as well as in material capital.
Just as land came to be seen as natural capital, human factors of production came to be seen as human capital.
Its role in growth and innovation is often cited to justify public subsidies for education and job training.
Unlike money capital, it tends to grow steadily and cumulatively over long periods, built on education and health.
It is intangible and cannot be owned by a firm, so it leaves when employees leave.
Gary Becker's human capital theory holds that investment in education and training raises efficiency and growth.

definition.text: The indexes used to compare countries' stocks of human capital.

facts.text: The World Bank's Human Capital Index, launched in October 2018, ranks countries by investment in young people's education and health care.
It harmonized learning data across 164 countries, measuring knowledge actually gained rather than years of schooling alone.
The World Economic Forum has published a Global Human Capital Index annually since 2012.
One measure of expected human capital put Finland highest at 28.4 adjusted years between ages 20 and 64, and Niger lowest at under 1.6.

title: Human capital and signaling

definition.text: The challenge to human capital theory from signaling theory, which says education may mark existing ability rather than create skills.

facts.text: Some labor economists criticize the Chicago-school theory for trying to explain all wage differences by human capital.
In Spence and Stiglitz's signaling theory, education lets able workers signal their ability to employers and earn higher wages.
Studies find wages also vary with gender, nativity, workplace discrimination and socioeconomic status.

contested_note: Human capital theory and signaling theory give rival explanations of why education raises wages.

definition.text: A single number that tracks how a group of related figures, such as prices or employment, changes over time.

facts.text: An index number compares a value with a base value, usually set at 100.
If a commodity's price doubles between 1960 and 1970, its index with 1960 as base is 200.
Examples include the consumer price index, cost-of-living index, stock market indices such as the S&P 500, and commodity indices.
Some indices compare places rather than times, such as purchasing power parity between currencies.
Index numbers turn complex data into easy-to-compare figures.

definition.text: The difficulty that statistical indices cannot perfectly measure economic change, because they rely on fixed assumptions such as a set basket of goods.

facts.text: Substitution bias arises when consumers switch to cheaper goods as prices rise, so the CPI misstates living costs.
The GDP deflator can skew real output by not fully adjusting for new products.
There is no perfect fix; baskets and weights are updated periodically, but long-term comparisons stay inexact.

definition.text: The total value of goods and services that businesses use up as inputs while producing, such as raw materials, services and other running costs.

facts.text: It equals the gap between gross output (roughly total sales value) and net output, that is gross value added or GDP.
Because it is subtracted from gross output to get GDP, how it is defined and estimated strongly affects the size of the GDP figure.
In the US economy, intermediate consumption is about 45% of gross output.
Inputs may be changed in form, like bulk sugar, or used up completely, like electric power.
Depreciation of fixed assets and major renovations that extend an asset's life are excluded; ordinary maintenance, repairs and research and development spending are included.
Buying a service from another firm instead of doing it in-house raises a firm's intermediate consumption and lowers its own value added.
If businesses buy physical assets GDP rises, while renting or leasing them lowers GDP, because lease payments count as intermediate consumption.

title: Imputed rent of owner-occupied housing

definition.text: The market rent that owner-occupiers would receive if their homes were rented out, which national accounts add to value added.

facts.text: Critics call this addition to GDP largely fictitious, since nearly all owner-occupiers do not actually rent out their homes.
The imputation rests on the idea that a dwelling provides its owner with a service.

contested_note: Critics argue the imputed rent added to GDP is largely fictitious.
notes: Section entry on the Intermediate consumption page; may be folded into a GDP criticisms entry.

definition.text: Committing resources, often money, to something expected to gain value over time.

facts.text: In finance, the aim of investing is to earn a return on the asset invested in.
The return can be a capital gain or loss when the asset is sold, or regular income such as dividends, interest or rent.
Investors usually expect higher returns from riskier investments, and low-risk investments generally earn low returns.
Spreading money across many investments, called diversification, reduces overall risk.
Common investments include stocks, bonds, cash, real estate, private equity and commodities.
Compared with savings, investments carry more kinds of risk and greater uncertainty.
Investments are often made through intermediaries such as pension funds, banks and insurance companies, which pool money from many investors.
Modern investing is usually dated to the 17th century, and the Amsterdam Stock Exchange began in 1602.

definition.text: In a national economy, spending in a year that adds to the country's stock of buildings, equipment, software and inventories.

facts.text: Net investment is gross investment minus depreciation; net fixed investment is the yearly net increase in the capital stock.
Investment is a flow measured over a period, while capital is a stock: the net investment accumulated up to a point in time.
It is often modelled as falling when interest rates rise, since interest is the cost of funds, and rising with income.
Some research models investment as rising with the gap between the profit-maximizing capital stock and the current one.
In classical theory, investment means producing goods that are not consumed right away but used to make other goods.
Investment is closely related to saving but is not the same thing.

title: Tobin's q

definition.text: The ratio between a physical asset's market value and the cost of replacing it, used to explain investment.

facts.text: When the ratio is above 1, a machine can be bought for less than the output it generates is worth, so firms gain by investing.

notes: No own article in crawl; section anchor on Investment (macroeconomics).

definition.text: The branch of economics that studies how a whole economy, regional, national or global, performs and behaves.

facts.text: Macroeconomists study economy-wide totals such as GDP, national income, unemployment, inflation, consumption, saving, investment and trade.
Its three central variables are output, unemployment and inflation.
It differs from microeconomics, which studies smaller units such as single firms, consumers and markets.
Its topics split by time frame: short-term swings of the business cycle, medium-term levels of variables such as unemployment, and long-term growth.
It also analyses monetary and fiscal policy, especially where they aim to stabilize the economy or its growth rate.
As a separate field it is usually dated to 1936, when Keynes published The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money.
Everything produced and sold generates an equal amount of income, and total net output is usually measured as GDP.
Since World War II, Keynesians, monetarists, new classical and new Keynesian economists have shaped mainstream research.

definition.text: Inflation is a general rise in prices across a whole economy; deflation is a general fall in prices.

facts.text: Economists measure these price changes with price indexes.
Inflation rises when an economy overheats and grows too fast, and a shrinking economy can push inflation down or into deflation.
Supply shocks also move inflation, for example the oil crises of the 1970s and the 2021–2023 global energy crisis.
High inflation and deflation both raise uncertainty, especially when unexpected, so most central banks aim for low, stable, positive inflation.
The quantity theory of money says price changes are caused by changes in the money supply, but it has proved unreliable over short and medium horizons.

definition.text: The state of people in the labour force who have no job but are actively looking for one, measured as a percentage called the unemployment rate.

facts.text: Retired people, students and discouraged job-seekers are outside the labour force and are not counted as unemployed.
Unemployment has a cyclical part that follows the business cycle and a lasting structural, or natural, part.
Okun's law links unemployment to short-run GDP growth; its original version says a 3% rise in output cuts unemployment by 1%.
Search, or frictional, unemployment arises because matching workers to vacancies takes time when information is imperfect.
Minimum wages, trade unions and efficiency wages can keep wages above the level where supply equals demand, causing some unemployment.

definition.text: The total amount of money in an economy, commonly measured as M1 and M2.

facts.text: M1 is liquid money such as cash, coins and checking deposits; M2 adds less liquid items such as time deposits, savings accounts and money market funds.
A liquid asset can be turned into cash quickly without much loss of value.
The money supply affects interest rates and is central to monetary policy.

definition.text: The school of thought begun by Keynes's General Theory, which explains why markets might not clear and stresses total demand as the driver of output.

facts.text: During the Great Depression, economists of the time struggled to explain how goods could go unsold and workers stay unemployed.
The older neoclassical view held that prices and wages would fall until all goods and labour were sold.
Keynes argued that a return to normal output would be slow at best, and he recommended active fiscal policy to stabilize demand and employment.
Keynes's followers merged his ideas with neoclassical microeconomics into the neoclassical synthesis, accepted by most economists by the 1950s.

definition.text: The way a change in spending is magnified as it passes through the economy, raising or lowering total output by more than the original change.

facts.text: Keynes explained how a small fall in consumption or investment could be magnified into declines across the economy.
A government-paid bridge adds its own value to output and also lets the workers spend and invest more, helping close an output gap.

definition.text: Milton Friedman's school of macroeconomics, which updated the quantity theory of money and stressed money's role in the economy.

facts.text: Friedman argued monetary policy was more effective than fiscal policy, but favoured steady money-supply growth over frequent intervention.
Friedman and Edmund Phelps denied a stable long-run trade-off between inflation and unemployment, a view supported by the 1970s oil shocks.
It was influential in the early 1980s but faded when central banks found money growth, inflation and real GDP growth too unstably linked to target money.

definition.text: The assumption, brought into macroeconomics by Robert Lucas, that people form forecasts using all current information about policy and conditions rather than just recent past trends.

facts.text: Before Lucas, economists used adaptive expectations, where people look only at the recent past.
In new classical models with rational expectations, monetary policy had only a limited effect.
The Lucas critique argued that models built on past statistical relationships fail when the underlying economy changes, and called for models with microeconomic foundations.

definition.text: A macroeconomic school that accepts rational expectations but shows how sticky prices and wages let monetary and fiscal policy affect real output.

facts.text: It traces sticky prices and wages to imperfect competition, so monetary policy changes quantities rather than only prices.
Stanley Fischer and John B. Taylor showed monetary policy could work even under rational expectations when contracts fix wages.

title: Endogenous growth theory

definition.text: Growth models from the 1980s and 1990s that explain growth from inside the economy, through increasing returns, learning-by-doing or firms' research, instead of outside technological change.

facts.text: Some versions model profit-seeking firms' research and development to explain technological progress.
It arose in the mid-1980s from dissatisfaction with models such as Solow–Swan, where long-run growth depends on unexplained technical progress.
It holds that the long-run growth rate depends on policy, such as subsidies for research or education that raise the incentive to innovate.
Knowledge spillovers, a kind of positive externality, keep returns to capital from falling to zero.

contested_note: Its explanatory power is disputed by critics, and ecological economists dispute its neglect of energy and materials.

title: Environment in macroeconomic models

definition.text: The inclusion of natural resource scarcity and climate change in macroeconomic models, especially growth models, to study their effects on the whole economy.

facts.text: Jevons's 1865 book The Coal Question argued that productivity gains could speed up resource scarcity in a growing economy.
During the 1970s oil crises, Stiglitz and Solow added non-renewable resources to growth models to ask whether living standards could keep rising.
The 2006 Stern Review gave the first comprehensive analysis of global economic damage from projected climate change.
Integrated assessment models, pioneered by William Nordhaus, are now widely used to estimate regional and global climate damages under different policies.
Such models treat land, water and energy as production inputs; Herman Daly's early work replaced the circular flow diagram with one driven by solar energy.
Methods for counting environmental goods and services in national accounts are still debated.

distinct_from: Source and sink functions of the environment

title: Source and sink functions of the environment

definition.text: The environment's two economic roles: as a source that supplies materials and services, and as a sink that absorbs and neutralizes waste and pollution.

facts.text: Natural inputs pass out of the economy as pollution and waste once they are consumed.
The source function is depleted as resources are used up or polluted.
When waste exceeds the sink's capacity to absorb it, long-term damage follows.
Ecological economics replaces the simple circular flow of income with a flow diagram in which solar energy sustains natural inputs and services used in production.
Once consumed, natural inputs leave the economy as pollution and waste.
The source function is run down as resources are used up or polluted.
When waste exceeds what the sink can absorb, long-term damage follows; some persistent pollutants such as nuclear waste are absorbed very slowly or not at all.

distinct_from: Costanza's valuation of the global ecosystem

definition.text: Short-run government and central-bank policy aimed at softening the harm done by business cycles, using fiscal and monetary tools.

facts.text: Policy is expansive in a recession and contractive when the economy overheats.
Longer-run structural policies instead target things like the structural unemployment rate or how much people save, invest and study.
Economists usually prefer monetary policy for moderate swings, since independent central banks face less political pressure and shorter lags.
Fiscal policy matters more after a major shock, in a liquidity trap, or under a fixed exchange rate.

definition.text: The reduction of private activity when government spending uses resources or raises interest rates, limiting fiscal policy's effect.

facts.text: Full crowding out happens when government spending simply replaces private output instead of adding to it.
Government spending that raises interest rates can also cut private investment.

definition.text: Parts of the tax and benefit system that cushion a downturn automatically, without new decisions by politicians.

facts.text: When unemployment rises, unemployment benefit spending rises and tax revenue falls, protecting part of private income and consumption.
They avoid the policy lags of discretionary fiscal policy.

definition.text: A common textbook model that finds the price level and real output where aggregate demand meets aggregate supply.

facts.text: The demand curve slopes down, so more output is demanded at lower price levels.
Near potential output, the full-employment level, extra demand only raises prices, not output.
Modern versions put inflation on the vertical axis, with an upward-sloping supply curve based on the Phillips curve.

definition.text: A model invented by John Hicks in 1936 showing the interest rates and output levels at which both the goods market and the money market are in balance.

facts.text: The goods market balances investment against saving (IS) and the money market balances money supply against money demand (LM).
It underpins the idea of aggregate demand by asking how much is demanded at a given price level.

definition.text: Branches of macroeconomics that reject mainstream theory, including ecological economics, modern monetary theory and Marxian economics.

facts.text: Heterodox economists see price flexibility, not price stickiness, as the source of instability, so they build models with different assumptions.

definition.text: The policy a nation's monetary authority uses to influence money and financial conditions in pursuit of goals such as high employment and low, stable inflation.

facts.text: Setting interest rates, directly or through open market operations, is generally its main tool.
Interest rate changes affect investment, consumption, asset prices and exchange rates, and so demand, employment and inflation; this is the monetary transmission mechanism.
Expansionary policy lowers rates to stimulate activity; contractionary policy dampens activity and inflation.
Most developed-country central banks target inflation, while most developing-country central banks target a fixed exchange rate.
Unlike fiscal policy, which uses taxes and government spending, it works through financial channels, and is usually run by central banks independent of government.
When interest rates are near zero, conventional policy cannot loosen further, so central banks may turn to quantitative easing.

title: Central bank
article: Monetary policy#Central banks and the gold standard

definition.text: A national bank that issues currency and sets interest rates, acting as lender of last resort to other banks.

facts.text: The Bank of England, created in 1694 with power to print gold-backed notes, began the idea of monetary policy independent of the executive.
Industrialized nations set up central banks between 1870 and 1920, the Federal Reserve among the last in 1913.
There is strong consensus that an independent central bank runs more credible monetary policy.

definition.text: A central bank's buying and selling of securities to influence interest rates, the exchange rate or the money supply.

facts.text: Buying a security such as a government bond in effect creates money, expanding the monetary base; selling securities shrinks it.
The monetary base is currency in circulation plus banks' reserves held at the central bank.

title: Quantitative easing
article: Monetary policy#Unconventional monetary policy at the zero bound

definition.text: Unconventional monetary policy used when interest rates are near zero, in which the central bank buys bonds and other assets to lower a wider range of interest rates.

facts.text: Unconventional tools include credit easing, quantitative easing, forward guidance and signalling.
Purchases can include government bonds, corporate bonds, stocks and other securities.
It is used because conventional policy can fail in a liquidity trap.

definition.text: Central banks' adjustment of monetary and supervisory policy to account for the effects of climate change.

facts.text: Central banks began considering climate effects on their frameworks around 2017–2018.
They argue climate change will add market volatility, inflation pressure from extreme weather or a disorderly transition, and financial risks.
The Network for Greening the Financial System, founded in 2017, has more than a hundred central banks and supervisors.
Proposals include green macro-prudential rules, green quantitative easing, green collateral rules and green refinancing operations.
In 2021 the European Central Bank said it would tilt its corporate bond purchases, a form of green QE, but it has not adopted a green interest rate.

definition.text: A complete and consistent set of accounts for measuring a nation's economic activity, built on double-entry bookkeeping.

facts.text: Double entry makes both sides of an account equal even though they measure different things, such as production and the income it generates.
They record output, spending and income of households, corporations and government, their links with other countries, and their net worth.
They present both flows over a period and stocks at the end of it, and reconcile the two.
GDP, perhaps the most widely cited measure of economic activity, is one of their aggregate measures.
They can be given in nominal or real amounts, real amounts removing the effect of price changes; growth rates are usually measured in real terms.
They are built from surveys, censuses and administrative data, and are usually compiled by national statistical offices or central banks, yearly and quarterly.
Colin Clark and Simon Kuznets made the first efforts in the late 1920s and 1930s, spurred by the Great Depression and Keynesian policy needs.
The United States published the first formal national accounts in 1947, and the UN published A System of National Accounts in 1952.

title: Main accounts of the national accounts

definition.text: The standard set of linked accounts that make up a nation's accounts: production, income, expenditure, capital and financial accounts, plus balance sheets.

facts.text: Each account has a balancing item: value added (equal to GDP for the whole economy), disposable income, saving, net lending or borrowing, and net worth.
Balance sheets record the stock of financial and non-financial assets and liabilities at a point in time.
Accounts can be gross or net of consumption of fixed capital, the national-accounts version of depreciation.

title: Unpaid work in national accounts

definition.text: The exclusion of unpaid work, such as household work, from every category of the national accounts and from GDP.

facts.text: An Australian study put the value of this uncounted work at about 50% of GDP.
Because GDP is tied to the national accounts, the omission may distort the picture they give.
Feminist economists such as Marilyn Waring and Nancy Folbre call the SNA biased for valuing no unpaid housework, though GDP imputes rent for owner-occupied homes.
Unpaid housework falls outside the SNA production boundary, which critics say hides how much market production depends on non-market labour.

contested_note: Feminist economists criticise the exclusion of unpaid work, while statisticians question whether valuing it is feasible.
distinct_from: Main accounts of the national accounts
notes: Also covers System of National Accounts#Feminist concerns.

definition.text: A method of valuing environmental assets, which ordinary measures of national wealth usually leave out, partly because they are hard to value.

facts.text: It is proposed as an alternative to treating environmental assets as worth zero.
It is also meant to measure whether welfare levels can be sustained when the environment is being degraded.
Methods for including environmental goods and services in national output are still under discussion.

definition.text: A method for measuring how social insurance shifts lifetime tax burdens between generations.

facts.text: It has been proposed as a better guide to whether fiscal policy is sustainable than the budget deficit, which only reflects one year's taxes minus spending.

definition.text: Gross national income minus depreciation.

facts.text: It covers the income of households, businesses and government.
It equals GDP plus net wages, salaries and property income from abroad, minus wear and tear of buildings, machinery, equipment and infrastructure.
By the expenditure method it is consumption plus investment plus government spending plus net exports, plus net foreign factor income, minus indirect taxes and depreciation of manufactured capital.

title: Adjusted net national income

definition.text: Net national income further reduced to account for the depletion of natural resources.

facts.text: The natural resources deducted are non-critical natural capital such as minerals.
It does not account for critical natural capital such as air and water.
Capital is split into manufactured capital, non-critical natural capital and critical natural capital, among other categories.
The European Environment Agency proposed using consumption of ecosystem capital to create an adjusted net national income.

notes: No page or section of its own; described in the Net national income lead and on Natural capital accounting.

definition.text: Gross national product minus depreciation; net domestic product is likewise GDP minus depreciation.

facts.text: Depreciation is the loss in value of fixed capital through wear and tear in production.
Economics research usually uses gross measures instead, a choice that has long been disputed.
It features in environmental economics as an indicator of sustainability and in models of natural resource depletion.
Research has studied it as a dynamic welfare indicator.

definition.text: A price index, developed by Étienne Laspeyres in 1871, that measures the cost of a fixed basket of base-period quantities at new prices.

facts.text: It often overstates inflation because it ignores consumers switching to cheaper goods when prices rise.
It is the easiest index to compute, needing only new price data, not new quantities.

definition.text: A price index, introduced by Hermann Paasche in 1874, that uses current-period quantities.

facts.text: It understates inflation by assuming consumers adjust their purchases instantly to new prices.
It needs current quantity data, so it is harder to compute than Laspeyres.

definition.text: A price index equal to the geometric mean of the Laspeyres and Paasche indices.

facts.text: It balances Laspeyres' tendency to overstate inflation and Paasche's tendency to understate it.
It is a superlative index, a class introduced by W. Erwin Diewert in 1976 and preferred for inflation and GDP measurement.

definition.text: Unweighted indices that compare prices of single items between periods, used as building blocks inside larger indices such as the CPI.

facts.text: The Carli index averages price ratios and is biased upward: a doubling and a halving give 1.25, not 1.
The Jevons index, from 1863, is the unweighted geometric mean of price relatives.

definition.text: A price index that updates its base every period and multiplies the period-to-period changes together.

facts.text: Unchained indices compare every period to one fixed base, so their bias grows over time as quantities drift.

definition.text: How efficiently goods or services are produced, usually measured as output per unit of input over a period.

facts.text: The most common measure is labour productivity, for example GDP per worker.
Measures using only one kind of input, such as worker hours, materials or energy per unit of output, are called partial productivities.
Rising national productivity can raise living standards, because higher wages let people buy more, enjoy leisure, and improve housing and education.
Productivity gains can go to workers as wages, owners as profits, consumers as lower prices, governments as taxes, and the environment when less resource or pollution is used per unit.
Simply adding inputs without productivity gains does not raise income per unit of input.
It depends on available technology and how resources are organized; the assembly line and electrification gave their biggest gains in the first decades after introduction.
National productivity grows through technological and organizational change, restructuring, economies of scale, research, education and competition.
Air pollution causes productivity losses through lost labour; with welfare losses, the World Bank put the global cost at over $8 trillion per year.

definition.text: Output volume, such as GDP or gross value added, divided by labour input, such as total hours worked or total employment.

facts.text: Output is usually measured as value added, the value of outputs minus intermediate inputs, to avoid double counting.
Total hours worked is generally preferred to a headcount, which can hide changes in average hours.
It is a key indicator of economic growth, competitiveness and living standards.
A country's ability to raise its living standards over time is said to depend almost entirely on raising output per worker.
Productivity can decouple from wages.

title: Productivity paradox

definition.text: The puzzle of slow overall productivity growth despite new technology, seen in the US from the 1970s to the early 1990s and again from the 2000s to the 2020s.

facts.text: Several causes have been proposed, but there is no consensus.
The debate now asks not just whether computers raise productivity but whether the potential for productivity growth is running out.

contested_note: There is no consensus on why productivity growth slowed.

title: Purchasing power parity

definition.text: A way of comparing currencies by what the same basket of goods costs in each country, giving an exchange rate based on purchasing power.

facts.text: It is used to compare countries' GDP, labour productivity, consumption and cost of living.
If a computer costs 500 US dollars in New York and 2000 HK dollars in Hong Kong, PPP implies 4 HK dollars per US dollar.
The OECD's basket covers around 3,000 consumer goods and services, 30 government occupations, 200 types of equipment and about 15 construction projects.
PPP rates suit comparisons of national production and consumption, where non-traded goods matter; market rates are used for individual traded goods.
Calculations are controversial because comparable baskets are hard to find and people in different countries buy different things.
The global poverty line is converted between currencies using PPP rates, though these are skewed by high-end goods that poor people rarely buy.
Emission intensities of economies can be calculated with either market exchange rates or PPP.

contested_note: PPP calculations are disputed because comparable baskets of goods are hard to find across countries.

definition.text: The principle that, without transport costs or trade barriers, a good should sell for the same price everywhere.

facts.text: It is the basis of purchasing power parity.
Transport costs and trade restrictions weaken it, by making goods expensive to move between countries.
Firms selling the same product at different prices in different markets also break it.

definition.text: A simple version of purchasing power parity whose basket contains a single good, a McDonald's Big Mac burger.

facts.text: The Economist created it in 1986 to teach economics and spot over- and under-valued currencies.
A Big Mac is perishable and hard to transport, so the law of one price is unlikely to hold for it.
One study found a correlation of 0.73 between its prices and prices from the Penn World Tables.

definition.text: The value of an economy's output adjusted to remove the effect of price changes, so it tracks the quantity produced.

facts.text: Because of inflation, nominal GDP can rise even when physical output stays the same.
Valuing every year's quantities at the prices of one base year makes differences reflect only changes in volume.
Dividing nominal GDP by real GDP gives the GDP deflator, which equals 100 in the base year and shows overall price change.
Annual real GDP growth is nominal GDP growth adjusted for inflation, usually given as a percentage.
It is also called constant GDP; organizations use different base years, such as UNCTAD's 2015 constant prices.
It is one example of the general distinction between real and nominal values in economics.

definition.text: Income that is not spent on immediate consumption; in economics, after-tax income minus consumption.

facts.text: Saving is an activity over time, a flow, while savings is an amount held at one moment, a stock.
Saving supplies the funds for investment: income not spent on consumer goods can be used to build factories and machinery, which supports growth.
More saving does not always mean more investment; it can instead cause a shortfall of demand and a recession.
In a simple farming economy, saving might mean holding back the best of the corn harvest as seed for next season.
In personal finance, saving means low-risk preservation of money, while investment carries higher risk of loss.
Capital markets balance personal saving, government surpluses and net exports against physical investment.

title: Saving and investment

definition.text: The question of whether interest rates automatically keep a nation's saving equal to its investment.

facts.text: Classical economics held that a rise in saving would lower interest rates and stimulate investment, so the two would always match.
Keynes argued both are insensitive to interest rates, so saving could exceed investment for long periods, causing a general glut and recession.
Keynes argued that savings withheld from investment cut total spending, incomes and jobs, which in turn reduces savings again.

contested_note: Classical economists and Keynes disagreed on whether interest rates keep saving and investment equal.

definition.text: The share of an extra unit of income that is saved; the share of total income saved is the average propensity to save.

facts.text: The saving rate is directly affected by the general level of interest rates.

definition.text: Networks of relationships, built on trust, shared norms and reciprocity, that help individuals and groups reach their goals.

facts.text: The earliest credited use of the term is by Lyda Hanifan in 1916, in an article on local support for rural schools; it became widely used in the late 1990s.
Pierre Bourdieu distinguished three forms of capital: economic, cultural and social.
Francis Fukuyama argues it forms through repeated interactions over time, is critical for development, and is hard to create through public policy.
Knack and Keefer (1996) found that trust and civic cooperation strongly affect economic growth across many countries.
Social networks and communities rich in social capital appear to protect health.
Scholars have criticised the concept as imprecisely defined.
Natural capital and social capital have each developed separate literatures as modern types of capital.

definition.text: Two main types of social capital: bonding ties within similar groups of people, and bridging ties between socially different groups.

facts.text: Criminal gangs create bonding social capital, while choirs and bowling clubs create bridging social capital.
Daniel Aldrich adds linking capital, the relationship between a person and a government official or elected leader.
Aldrich applies these ideas to disaster recovery, studying Japan after the 2011 Fukushima meltdown.
Negative effects of social capital are more often linked to bonding than to bridging.

title: Negative social capital

definition.text: The harmful side of social capital, where strong group ties produce bad outcomes for society.

facts.text: Research has linked civic associations to the rise of fascist movements.
Bourdieu showed how social connections can be used to reproduce inequality by giving access to powerful positions.
Without bridging ties, bonding groups can become isolated from the rest of society.

contested_note: Putnam sees social capital as positive, while a sizable literature finds it can have adverse effects.

title: Measuring social capital

definition.text: The disputed task of quantifying social capital, using tools such as trust surveys, network name generators and counts of group membership.

facts.text: There is no widely held consensus on how to measure it, which has become a debate in itself.
It is hard to measure partly because it emerges across levels as individuals take part in groups, rather than being held by any one person.
The UN Sustainable Development Group's World Social Capital Monitor uses anonymous surveys of trust, solidarity and willingness to fund public goods, starting in 2016.

contested_note: There is no consensus on how social capital should be measured.

title: Stock and flow

definition.text: The distinction between a stock, a quantity existing at one point in time, and a flow, a quantity measured per unit of time.

facts.text: GDP is a flow measured in dollars per year, while a nation's capital stock is a stock measured in dollars.
The capital stock is increased by the flow of new investment and depleted by the flow of depreciation.
Capital is a stock that yields a periodic income, which is a flow.
Stocks and flows have different units, so they cannot be added or compared, though their ratios are meaningful: debt to GDP is measured in years.
If a country has 20 machines on 1 January 2010 and 23 a year later, net investment during 2010 was 3 machines per year.
Irving Fisher formalized the distinction in economics in 1896, and Michał Kalecki called economics 'the science of confusing stocks with flows'.

distinct_from: Stocks and flows in environmental systems

title: Stocks and flows in environmental systems

definition.text: The use of stocks, which build up through inflows and drain through outflows, to describe natural systems such as the atmosphere, the carbon cycle and reservoirs.

facts.text: Climate change mitigation is a stock-and-flow problem: cut the stock of greenhouse gases in the air by reducing emissions and increasing carbon dioxide removal.
Earth system science is full of stock-and-flow problems, such as the carbon, nitrogen and water cycles and Earth's energy budget.
Carbon dioxide in the atmosphere is a stock measured in tons, raised by emissions and lowered by sequestration, both in tons per day.
Stocks and flows are the basic building blocks of system dynamics models; Jay Forrester called them levels and rates.
Mathematically, a stock is the accumulation of inflows minus outflows over time.

title: System of National Accounts

definition.text: The international standard set of concepts and methods for compiling national accounts, known until 1993 as the United Nations System of National Accounts.

facts.text: Almost every country uses it; it has been adopted in more than 200 countries, territories and areas, often with local adaptations.
Following it improves data quality and comparability between countries and over time.
The UN published the first standard in 1953, with revisions in 1960, 1964, 1968, 1993 and 2008; SNA 2025 is due to be published in 2026.
Using it is voluntary, though the UN has encouraged national statistics offices to apply it since 1953.
Early national accounting aimed at estimating national income and wealth; the first known attempt in England was by William Petty in 1665.
A global standard was first proposed at the League of Nations in 1928, but the work was interrupted by World War 2.
Its most common criticism is that its concepts and classifications do not adequately reflect real-world activities and relationships.

distinct_from: Greening the System of National Accounts

title: Greening the System of National Accounts

definition.text: The half-century effort, and debate, to bring the natural environment, resource depletion and ecosystem services into the System of National Accounts.

facts.text: Critics argued the SNA ignored the natural environment that contains and supports the economy, and did not value resource stocks, their depletion, or ecosystem services.
Leaving out pollution costs meant national accounts overstated the net benefits of economic activity.
SNA 1993 first introduced environmental satellite accounts, and the System of Environmental-Economic Accounting (SEEA) followed the 1992 Rio Earth Summit.
SNA 1993 also introduced a depletion-adjusted net domestic product, though not formally within the framework.
The SEEA Central Framework became a UN standard in February 2012.
SNA 2025 formally recognizes natural capital and ecosystem services and treats resource depletion as a production cost.
In early 2025 at least 94 countries had produced at least one SEEA account in the past five years, 67 of them regularly.

contested_note: Environmentalists argue the SNA still undervalues nature, while statisticians note that measurement methods remain unsettled.

title: Satellite accounts
article: System of National Accounts#Satellite accounts and supplementary tables

definition.text: Extra accounts linked to the core national accounts that give detail on a topic, such as the environment, without changing the core accounts.

facts.text: Non-core accounts are in principle optional, and countries produce them when there is demand and budget.
SNA 2008 recognized environmental satellite accounts such as material flow, emission and energy accounts.

title: Total factor productivity

definition.text: The ratio of total output, such as GDP, to total inputs, also called multi-factor productivity; it measures how much output a given amount of inputs yields.

facts.text: Its growth is the part of output growth not explained by growth in measured labour and capital inputs, so it is calculated as a residual.
It is calculated by dividing output by a weighted geometric average of labour and capital, usually weighted 0.7 for labour and 0.3 for capital.
For small changes, its growth rate is roughly output growth minus the growth rates of labour and capital inputs.
In a Cobb–Douglas production function, output depends on total factor productivity (A), capital (K) and labour (L).
Easterly and Levine estimated in 2001 that it accounts for 60 percent of growth in output per worker for an average country.
Robert Solow (1957) described it as 'technical change', a shorthand for any shift in the production function.
Official statisticians prefer the term multifactor productivity because inputs such as energy are usually left out, as are costs like mineral depletion and pollution.
Critics say it lacks meaningful units and may be a modelling artefact; growth accounting is also open to the Cambridge critique.

contested_note: Some economists consider TFP and growth accounting invalid or in need of careful interpretation.

title: Growth accounting

definition.text: A method that splits economic growth into the parts due to more inputs, such as labour and capital, and the part due to technological change.

facts.text: Multi-factor productivity is typically estimated using growth accounting.
National accounts data are used for growth accounting over long periods to estimate sources of growth.
Growth accounting and total factor productivity are open to the Cambridge critique, so some economists doubt the method's validity.

notes: No page of its own in crawl; mentioned on Productivity, National accounts and Total factor productivity.

definition.text: The finding that much of measured productivity growth tracks energy use and how efficiently energy is converted into useful work.

facts.text: There is a historical correlation between total factor productivity and energy use and conversion efficiency.
Reiner Kümmel concluded that the Solow residual can be explained very well by an economy's energy input.
On this view, technical progress is the ability to absorb primary energy and convert it efficiently into useful energy for production.

definition.text: The difference between the market value of a product or service and the value of the inputs used to make it.

facts.text: A firm's total value added equals its revenue minus intermediate consumption.
It roughly equals pay to employees, a return to labour, plus earnings before taxes, a return to capital.
In macroeconomics, it is the contribution of capital and labour to a product's value, so national value added is shared between them.
In national accounts, gross value added is gross output minus intermediate consumption, which equals net output.
Net value added deducts depreciation from gross value added.
For the whole economy at market prices, gross value added equals GDP.

definition.text: A tax on sales that is charged at each stage of production on the value that stage adds.

facts.text: It is assessed step by step on a product or service, taxing each stage's unit value added.

definition.text: Money and other resources measured in money that businesses use to buy what they need to produce goods or services.

facts.text: It comes from a firm's retained earnings or from lenders and investors, and is used to buy real capital equipment.
Real capital, by contrast, is physical goods that help produce other goods, such as sewing machines for tailors.
Lenders provide financial capital for a price: interest.
Fixed capital buys lasting assets, while working capital pays for stock, expenses and credit.
Some ecological economists want natural capital added to the usual analysis of land, labour and financial capital.
Commodity markets are affected by factors that influence natural capital, such as weather affecting food crops.

definition.text: The ratio between a business's borrowed capital (debt) and its own capital (equity).

facts.text: Own capital comes from owners, for example through savings or inheritance; borrowed capital comes through debt and must usually be repaid with interest.
High leverage can bring higher profit but creates a risk of insolvency.
